p.title: Universal multilayer network exploration by random walk with restart

ext.title: Universal multilayer network exploration by random walk with restart
ext.document_type: Journal research article (open access, CC BY 4.0), with methods and supplementary material referenced but supplementary notes not in the extracted text
ext.coverage: Read all 1277 lines of the extracted text (abstract, introduction, results including the RWR formalism, numerical implementation, LOOCV and link-prediction evaluations, parameter-space exploration, discussion, data/code availability, figure captions, references 1-34, back matter). Supplementary Notes 1-5 and Figs S9-S16 are cited but not in the file, so their contents are not covered. Metadata hint corrected: full author list is Anthony Baptista, Aitor Gonzalez, Anais Baudot; article number 170.
ext.research_question: Can random walk with restart (RWR) be generalized to explore any combination of multiplex, monoplex and bipartite networks (a "universal multilayer network"), and how do added network layers and bipartite links change prediction performance and the stability of outputs to input parameters?
ext.theory: Random walks as iterative stochastic processes on graphs; RWR as a steady-state diffusion / personalized PageRank measuring proximity of all nodes to seed(s) (p.1-2, citing Lovasz 1993, Brin and Page 1998, Gomez et al. 2013). Multilayer formalism following De Domenico et al. 2013 and Kivela et al. 2014: supra-adjacency matrices for multiplex layers (with inter-layer jump probability delta), bipartite matrices for heterogeneous links, and a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with inter-network jump probabilities lambda and restart parameters eta (network) and tau (layer) (Eqs 5-16, Fig. 2, p.2-4). No behavioural or social theory is used.
ext.data: Two empirical multilayer networks, no sample sizes given in the main text. (1) Biological network: a gene multiplex (gene physical and functional relationships), a drug multiplex (drug clinical and chemical relationships), and a disease monoplex (phenotypic similarity), linked by gene-disease, drug-gene and drug-disease bipartite networks (p.4, detailed in Supplementary Note 3.B). Unit: genes, drugs, diseases as nodes. (2) Airports network: French, British and German airport multiplex networks (nodes = airports; edges = national flight connections for three airline companies), linked by French-German, British-German and French-British transnational bipartite networks (p.4, Supplementary Note 3.A). Node and edge counts, time period and original sources are not stated in the main text. Data and code are on OSF (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZSMUA) and GitHub (anthbapt/multixrank). Comparison dataset in Methods: the PPI network (p.4-5).
ext.method: Formal: derivation of RWR on universal multilayer networks (Eqs 1-16), with the normalization generalized from Li and Patra 2010 and Valdeolivas et al. 2018 to N multiplex networks. Implemented as the Python package MultiXrank (optimized, pip installable; complexity analysis in Supplementary Note 2). Evaluation: (a) Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV): each known gene-disease association left out in turn, remaining associations used as seeds, rank of left-out gene recorded and CDF of ranks plotted (p.4-5, Fig. 3a-b). (b) Link Prediction (LP): a gene-disease edge removed and its gene ranked with the disease as seed (p.6, Figs S11, S14). (c) Controls: artificially added transit drug nodes linking gene-disease pairs (1, 2 or 5 per association; Fig 3c-d) and progressive random rewiring of the enhanced bipartite networks (p.5-6). (d) Parameter-space exploration: 125 parameter sets; pairwise similarity of rank output between parameter sets (Eqs 17-18, rank-based distance normalized across multiplex networks), PCA projection, k-means on first two PCs, comparison of top-5 and top-100 nodes per cluster (p.6-8, Fig. 4).
ext.identification: No causal identification strategy. Predictive performance is assessed against held-out known associations (LOOCV and LP). Causal-style claims about bipartite overlap are made by artificially manipulating bipartite connectivity (transit nodes) and then randomizing edges (p.5-6). Stability of outputs is assessed by varying parameters across 125 sets (p.7).
ext.scope: Methodological paper. Two example networks only: a biological gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. No population or institution; the airport network is a current-era transport network and the biological network is drawn from unspecified databases. Claims of general applicability (social, economic, ecological networks, p.8) are not tested in the paper.

key_findings.finding: RWR is generalized to universal multilayer networks by a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix, with inter-multiplex jump parameters lambda and restart parameters eta and tau. The normalization is the step the authors describe as previously unsolved beyond two heterogeneous multiplex networks.
key_findings.location: Results, Eqs 10-16, p.3-4; Introduction p.2 (normalization unsolved for N multiplex networks)
key_findings.numbers: Parameters delta, lambda, eta, tau; sum of lambda over alpha = 1 for each beta; sum over j of tau_kj = 1

key_findings.finding: In the gene-disease LOOCV, combining the gene multiplex with the disease monoplex improves ranking over PPI alone and over the gene multiplex alone. Adding the drug multiplex does not further improve performance.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values given in text; comparison is by CDF curves

key_findings.finding: In the airports network, adding the German multiplex (with French-German and British-German bipartites) increases RWR's ability to predict French-British airport associations, unlike the drug addition in the biological network.
key_findings.numbers: Three networks: French, British, German airport multiplexes

key_findings.finding: Bipartite overlap explains the difference: only 23% of genes in the gene-disease bipartite network appear in the drug-gene bipartite, and only 5% of diseases appear in the disease-drug bipartite. The airport bipartites show high overlap.
Artificially adding transit drug nodes that link existing gene-disease associations raises LOOCV performance drastically, and the same holds for the airport network.
key_findings.numbers: 1, 2 or 5 transit nodes per gene-disease association (biological); 1, 2 or 5 transit German nodes per French-British association (airports); no performance values in text

key_findings.finding: Progressively randomizing the enhanced bipartite networks continuously lowers LOOCV performance, down to the level of using only two multiplex networks.
key_findings.numbers: Randomization runs to completely random bipartite networks; no values in text

key_findings.finding: Link prediction gives behaviour similar to LOOCV.
key_findings.location: Evaluations, p.6, Figs S11 and S14 (supplementary)

key_findings.finding: Output sensitivity to input parameters differs by network. Top-ranked gene nodes vary more than top-ranked disease nodes across 125 parameter sets. The biological gene-disease network has stable regions, while the airport network has highly variable top-rankings.
key_findings.location: Parameter space exploration, p.6-8, Fig. 4a-c; Supplementary Figs S15-S16
key_findings.numbers: 125 parameter sets; PCA space; 8 clusters; clusters 4 and 6 give similar top-100 nodes

key_findings.finding: Authors conclude that more network data does not always increase predictive power, and that bipartite network connectivity is critical.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1; Results p.5-6; Discussion p.7

limitations: Paper has no dedicated limitations section; limitations stated in text: the formalism for some universal networks 'might sometimes require some adaptations' (Discussion, p.7).
Billion-scale networks are not handled; the authors name BEAR (exact or approximate) and BEPI (approximate) as strategies to consider (Discussion, p.8).
Performance on the biological network depends on bipartite overlap, which is low for drug-gene and disease-drug links (23% and 5%) (p.5-6).
Parameter-space stability differs by network (airport network variable; biological network stable in some regions) (p.8).
Only two example networks are evaluated (p.4-8).

rel.summary_md:
Baptista, Gonzalez and Baudot (2022) extend random walk with restart (RWR, a seed-personalized PageRank) to "universal" multilayer networks. These combine any number of multiplex networks, where the same nodes appear on several layers, linked by bipartite networks. They build one column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with separate dials for layer jumps (delta), jumps between networks (lambda) and restart allocation (eta, tau). The method ships as the MultiXrank Python package.

They test it with leave-one-out ranking (LOOCV) and link prediction on two examples: a gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. In the biological network, adding the drug multiplex did not help. The cause was low bipartite overlap: only 23% of genes and 5% of diseases are shared across the bipartite links. In the airport network, adding the German layer did help, because overlap there is high. Adding artificial transit nodes raised performance, and gradually randomizing those links lowered it again. Across 125 parameter sets, top-ranked outputs were stable in parts of the biological network and very unstable in the airport network.

Three parts of Paul's system are close to this. The staffer network's layer-balanced PageRank already runs a random walk over several layers: each node splits its transition mass equally across its active layers, and teleport is balanced across entity kinds. However, it checks sensitivity only on damping (0.70/0.85/0.95), never on how mass is split across layers. The Congress multilayer builder merges the cosponsor, engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance layers into a single edge weight, so it has no layer-jump parameter. No held-out test checks whether each added layer improves anything; the only per-layer evidence is null neighbour co-movement on the cosponsor and HCoI layers. The paper's main lesson for this system is to test whether each layer earns its place, and how much its links overlap with the base graph, before treating more layers as more signal. It gives no evidence about legislatures, lobbying or social ties.

bearings.paper_claim: In a multiplex-heterogeneous random walk, top-ranked nodes can shift a lot as inter-layer and inter-network jump and restart parameters change. Across 125 parameter sets the biological network had stable regions but the airport network's top rankings were highly variable. The stability of a given network has to be measured, not assumed.
bearings.paper_location: Parameter space exploration, p.6-8, Eqs 17-18, Fig. 4a-c
bearings.system_side: Builds a bidirectional row-stochastic walk in which each node gives 1/active_layers of its mass to each active layer, then splits it in proportion to weight within the layer. Teleport mass is equal across entity kinds. PageRank is computed at damping 0.70, 0.85 and 0.95, with L1 distance and top-1000 overlap against 0.85. The equal-layer split is labelled an explicit modelling prior, but it is never varied, and the per-kind teleport split is never varied either.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The math transfers directly, because both are stochastic walks over typed layers and node kinds. The empirical stability result does not: it comes from biology and airport data, and the authors found that stability depends on the network. So the paper argues for running a layer-allocation and teleport-split sweep on the staffer graph itself. It says nothing about which allocation is right. Scores remain descriptive connectedness, never access or introduction probabilities (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Adding a network layer improved LOOCV ranking only when its bipartite links overlapped the existing structure. In the airport network, overlap was high and the added layer helped. In the biological network, only 23% of genes and 5% of diseases were shared, and the added drug layer did not help. Gradually randomizing the boosted bipartite links pushed performance back down to the two-network baseline. The authors conclude that more network data is not always better.
bearings.paper_location: Evaluations p.4-7, Fig. 3a-d, Fig. S13; Discussion p.7
bearings.system_side: Merges the engagement, HCoI, social and (holistic config) co-appearance layers into one monoplex edge weight. Under the CU config, media edges are admitted only for pairs with no existing tie, HCoI edges only when they touch a cosponsor-isolated member, and social edges also reinforce existing ties by multiplication. Under the holistic config, a tied pair takes the max of cosponsor and media weights. Layer identity survives only on a provenance sheet that the engine never reads. No per-layer held-out test of predictive gain is recorded. The one per-layer test, neighbour co-movement, was null on both cosponsor (52%) and HCoI (49%).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over as a design principle: test each layer's gain on a held-out task and report its overlap with the base graph. The specific numbers (23%, 5%) are from biology and do not transfer. The paper's layers keep their identity in a supra-adjacency matrix. Melange's builder merges them into one weight, so the paper's per-layer jump parameters have no counterpart in the code. Gains and losses for Melange stay UNVERIFIED until measured on congressional data (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: RWR propagates proximity from seed nodes over multiple hops and across layers, and was evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation (each known association held out and ranked). Combining layers beat a single interaction layer in the gene-disease task, but only for layers with high overlap.
bearings.paper_location: Results Eqs 1-16 p.2-4; LOOCV p.4-5, Fig. 3a
bearings.system_side: Stance imputation is the mean tier score of a member's direct neighbours on one graph layer: at least 5 neighbours, |est| >= 0.75, giving 307 proposals. Its masking check gives 77% sign agreement. The HCoI layer is used only for the co-movement test, not for imputation.
bearings.code_ref: fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:90 (single-layer adjacency), fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py:133-148 (one-hop neighbour mean + masking validation)
bearings.transfer_conditions: A per-member RWR seeded on known stances, run on the cosponsor graph or the cosponsor plus HCoI layers, could replace the one-hop mean. The existing masking protocol already has the same form as the paper's LOOCV. Neighbour co-movement was null on both layers, so a multi-hop walk may not help either. Treat this as a candidate needing a prereg and a single look, not as evidence. Stance labels are Paul's domain: proposals only, and the matrix is never edited.

bearings.paper_claim: RWR scores how close every node is to a seed by summing over all walks rather than a single path. RWR has been shown to outperform local distance measures for gene-disease prioritization.
bearings.paper_location: Introduction p.2 (citing Kohler et al. 2008); Results p.2-4
bearings.system_side: Uses most-reliable-path Dijkstra on -log p, with chainHold equal to the product of activeP along one chain (ASKM 0.07). bestSponsors ranks pro members by the reliability of their single best chain to the target.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An RWR score seeded at the target, or at the pro-sponsor set, would add a multi-route robustness measure alongside the single best path. That fits the robustness to losing a node that Paul wants. The paper's support for RWR comes from biological prioritization, not recruitment, and gives no congressional estimate. Any such score is a heuristic proximity, never an ask-success or access probability (D-025).

gaps_exposed: No per-layer held-out evaluation, such as leave-one-out or link prediction, of whether the engagement, HCoI, social or co-appearance layers improve any prediction over the cosponsor-only graph. The builder logs admission counts, not predictive gain.

No measure of overlap or connectivity between the media layers and the cosponsor base. This is the quantity the paper says decides whether a layer helps. Recorded media shares (1.5% of holistic pairs vs 28.8% of CU pairs) are admission statistics, not an overlap test.
The Congress multilayer graph is merged into one weight per pair, so there is no per-layer walk or jump parameter and no way to switch a layer's contribution up or down without a rebuild.

The staffer PageRank sensitivity harness varies only damping. The equal-active-layer split and the per-kind teleport split, both called modelling priors, are never swept or checked for top-k stability.
No randomization control: rewiring a layer's edges to check that its contribution is structural rather than an artifact of density.
flags: Do not read 'more network data is not always better' as support for dropping regular cosponsorship edges. That proposal was measured and REJECTED in this project, and the paper's claim concerns whole added layers with low bipartite overlap, not edge classes within the cosponsor layer.

The paper's column normalization is the standard stochastic normalization of a walk operator, as in the staffer layer_balanced_transition. It is not per-edge volume normalization of cosponsorship weights, which was measured and REJECTED. Do not cite this paper for it.

If RWR or PageRank outputs are adopted anywhere (staffer connectedness, recruitment proximity, stance imputation), they are heuristic model outputs and never closeness, access or introduction probabilities (D-025). Any rank figure must name its window and denominator.
Any claimed gain from adding layers or switching to RWR stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). The paper's own evidence is limited to biology and airport networks.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's annotations record no takeaways for this paper. Both bibliography entries list it as citation-only, in the Path-Finding Algorithums folder, with only a title-level cross-reference to multilayer social-graph exploration. The one substantive position is a highlight, attached to melange-sna.multilayer-social-press-edges, that more layers are not always better. The paper supports that reading, and it is more relevant now than Paul's note suggests. Since he read it, the system has added several media layers and a holistic co-appearance layer through max or dominance admission without any per-layer predictive test. His filing it under path-finding fits a proximity-ranking alternative to single best-path Dijkstra, but nothing in his notes connects it to the staffer layer-balanced PageRank, which is the closest built analogue.

related.why: Source of the HCoI shared-issue-attention layer, one of the layers whose added value Baptista's overlap and ablation logic would test.
Grounds the social (repost and mention) layer that is merged into the multilayer cosponsor graph.
Link-prediction evaluation of network proximity measures; Baptista uses link prediction alongside LOOCV to score RWR.
Most-reliable single-path ranking, which the recruitment path uses, versus RWR's sum over all walks. The two are alternative ways to score proximity from a seed.
Compares centrality forms (Katz over PageRank) on legislative networks. RWR is personalized PageRank, so the choice between the two applies directly.
Makes a parallel 'more data is not always better' argument, about bias in social-network-site data.
Another higher-order or heterogeneous representation of lobby networks, where the question of layer and bipartite structure comes up again.
Bipartite lobbying-to-legislator network. Baptista shows bipartite connectivity decides whether a heterogeneous walk adds information.
